entries.title: 🆚 C++ vs C - Key Differences
tips: Add `using namespace std;` to avoid typing `std::` everywhere (but avoid in headers).
`std::endl` flushes the buffer; `\n` is faster if you don't need flushing.

entries.title: 📦 Canonical Form - The 42 Standard
entries.content:
42 requires the Orthodox Canonical Class Form (OCCF). You must explicitly define 4 things for your classes:

1. Default Constructor
2. Copy Constructor
3. Copy Assignment Operator
4. Destructor

```cpp
class Dog {
public:
    Dog();                                 // Default constructor
    Dog(const Dog& other);                 // Copy constructor
    Dog& operator=(const Dog& other);      // Copy assignment operator
    ~Dog();                                // Destructor
};
```

- The Rule of Three - If you need to write a custom destructor, you almost certainly need a custom copy constructor and assignment operator.
tips: Use member initializer lists in constructors for efficiency.
Always make destructors `virtual` in base classes!

entries.title: 🧬 Templates - Generic Coding
tips: Template errors can be very long - read the first line of the error closely.
Use `typename` instead of `class` in the template parameter list (it's identical but clearer).

entries.title: 🧰 The STL - Smart Containers
tips: `std::vector` is almost always better than a raw array.
Use iterators to loop through STL containers efficiently.

entries.title: 🛡️ Casting - The Safe Quartet
tips: Avoid `reinterpret_cast` unless absolutely necessary (like low-level hardware or parsing raw bytes).
`dynamic_cast` returns `nullptr` (or throws `std::bad_cast` for references) if the cast fails.

entries.title: 📌 Refs vs Pointers
entries.content:
References are aliases for existing variables. They are safer than pointers.

```cpp
int x = 10;
int &ref = x;    // ref IS x
ref = 20;        // x is now 20
```

- When to use references - When a parameter must always refer to a valid object. References cannot be null and cannot be reassigned.
- When to use pointers - When you need to iterate over arrays, reassign the target, or if `nullptr` is a valid, expected state.

- Enter `nullptr` - Never use `NULL` or `0` for pointers in modern C++. Use `nullptr`, which has a specific pointer type and prevents overload resolution errors.
```cpp
int* ptr = nullptr;
```
tips: Pass large objects as `const Type&` to avoid expensive copies.
Always initialize pointers to `nullptr` if they don't have a value yet.

entries.title: 🧠 C++ Memory Map & new/delete
tips: If you use `new[]`, you must use `delete[]`.
Memory leaks occur if you lose the pointer before calling `delete`.
